description: Space Dev's is a team of curious builders passionate about coding, SI, science and space. We're creating SOLARA, a Mars exploration platform combining NASA data, terrain analysis, rover imagery and environmental insights integrated with SI for mission planning.
summary:
SOLARA is an interactive Mars exploration and mission-planning platform developed by Space Dev's for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It brings planetary imagery, scientific datasets, rover information, and terrain analysis together in one interface, helping users explore the Martian surface and better understand potential exploration sites.

Inspired by the challenge of planning human exploration on Mars, SOLARA aims to make complex scientific information easier to access, interpret, and use. Users can explore Martian terrain, investigate locations, examine elevation and slope, view rover imagery, and evaluate potential routes. Our vision also includes an AI-powered Mission Copilot that helps interpret scientific data and provide context for exploration decisions.

SOLARA is important because successful Mars exploration requires understanding the environment before making decisions. By combining NASA data with interactive visualization and analytical tools, we aim to make planetary science more accessible and support better-informed Mars exploration planning.
details:
# SOLARA — Interactive Mars Exploration and Preliminary Mission Planning

SOLARA is an interactive Mars exploration and preliminary mission-planning platform designed to make planetary science data easier to explore, understand and use. It brings multiple sources of Martian scientific information into one workspace, allowing users to explore the planet through an interactive 3D globe and a detailed surface map.

**Source Code**

https://github.com/codeenginexofficial/solara/

**What exactly does it do?**

SOLARA allows users to navigate different regions of Mars, explore available orbital imagery, examine elevation and topography, view geological information, and investigate rover locations, traverses and imagery where available. It brings these different types of scientific information together so users can develop a better understanding of Martian locations without having to navigate multiple disconnected resources.

The platform also provides terrain-analysis capabilities, including elevation and slope information, to help users examine the physical characteristics of potential exploration areas. Its preliminary route-planning system uses available terrain information to help evaluate possible traverses. These routes are exploratory estimates, not validated paths for real rover operations.

**How does it work?**

SOLARA combines planetary data services, interactive mapping and computational tools in a single application. Users can select a location or region on Mars, activate available scientific layers and inspect the information associated with that area.

The application uses orbital imagery, elevation and topographic information, geological layers and rover-related records to provide geographical and scientific context. Data availability and resolution vary depending on the source and region.

SOLARA also includes an optional AI-powered Mission Copilot prototype, supported by OpenRouter. It is designed to help users ask questions, understand available mission context and receive assistance with preliminary exploration and planning. Its responses depend on the information and tools available to the application, so AI-generated explanations are not treated as authoritative scientific conclusions.

**What benefits does it have?**

SOLARA helps reduce the difficulty of exploring planetary science information spread across different platforms. By bringing mapping, scientific layers, terrain analysis and rover-related information into one workspace, it makes Mars exploration more accessible and helps users investigate locations more efficiently.

It can benefit students, educators, researchers and people interested in planetary exploration by providing an interactive way to understand Martian geography, examine scientific information and explore potential mission locations.

**What do we hope to achieve?**

Our goal is to demonstrate how different planetary science resources can be integrated into a single, accessible exploration environment. We hope SOLARA can support scientific learning, encourage interest in planetary research and provide a foundation for more advanced mission-planning tools.

Our long-term vision is to expand the platform's scientific coverage, improve terrain analysis and route-planning capabilities, and make more of the Martian surface accessible through one integrated scientific workspace.

**What tools, programming languages, hardware and software did we use?**

SOLARA was developed using React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS for the application interface. CesiumJS supports 3D planetary visualization, while OpenLayers provides interactive 2D mapping and scientific layer exploration.

Cloudflare Workers provide backend functionality, and OpenRouter supports the optional AI Mission Copilot integration. The project incorporates publicly available planetary science data and services, including NASA and USGS resources, with datasets such as orbital imagery, elevation information, geological layers and rover-related records.

The project was developed as a software-based platform and does not require specialised physical hardware beyond a computer capable of running the application and accessing its data services.

**What makes SOLARA creative and innovative?**

SOLARA combines interactive planetary visualization, scientific data exploration, terrain analysis, preliminary route planning and AI-assisted interaction in one workspace. Rather than treating these capabilities as separate tools, it brings them into a connected exploration workflow.

Throughout development, our team considered scientific accuracy, data availability, spatial resolution, usability, performance and accessibility. We also considered the limitations of individual datasets, recognising that missing observations or differences in data coverage should not be mistaken for complete scientific knowledge.

SOLARA is a prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It is not an official NASA product, and its preliminary route-planning results are not intended for real-world rover navigation or safety decisions.
